text: The source compares three common ways to harvest rice, each with different trade-offs. Manual harvesting with a sickle (ការច្រូតដោយដៃ) needs no fuel or machinery, can be done in wet or muddy fields where machines cannot go, and works for any field size or shape, but is slow, labor-intensive, and — because it takes longer to finish a field — leaves cut rice exposed to weather and pests for longer, which can add to losses if harvest is delayed by lack of labor. A reaper/mower machine (ម៉ាស៊ីនច្រូតផ្ដល) cuts the standing rice and lays it in windrows but does not thresh it, so cut rice still needs to be gathered, bundled, and carried to a threshing point afterward; it works fastest on relatively dry, firm ground and speeds up the cutting step considerably compared to hand harvesting, cited in the source in the range of roughly 2-4 hectares per day depending on the model and field conditions. A combine harvester (ម៉ាស៊ីនច្រូតកំបេ / ម៉ាស៊ីនច្រូតបែបផ្សំ) cuts, threshes, and cleans the grain in a single pass through the field, cutting total harvest-to-threshing time dramatically and reducing the field-exposure losses that come with manual methods, but it costs much more to own or hire, needs reasonably dry and accessible fields to operate well, and can produce more broken or unthreshed grain if not properly adjusted for the variety and moisture condition of the crop. In practice, many Cambodian farmers mix methods — for example hand-harvesting small or waterlogged plots and hiring a combine service for larger, drier fields — based on field access, labor availability, and cost. (Note: the capacity figures given here — hectares per day or per hour — are illustrative examples from the source and vary by machine model, field condition, and operator experience; get current rates from an actual machine or service provider before planning around them.)
